item.title: Get Good Grades in College but Make at Least One Friend Too
item.description:
Friends

Get Good Grades in College but Make at Least One Friend Too

Students don't need to win a popularity contest but do need at least one friend.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • College students have elevated rates of loneliness.
  • Structured befriending activities can help form friendships.
  • Having one friend helps bolster well-being and mental health.
Students connecting during an on-campus therapy dog visit
Source: Freya L. L. Green Photography; Used with permission

"Young adults are inundated with ideas that the college experience will be the best 4 years of their lives, but research has demonstrated that students often feel their actual experiences are different than what they expected (Moeller & Seehuus, 2019; Richardson et al., 2017), causing a lack of quality of their social connections (Larson et al., 1982; Laursen & Hartl, 2013; Lim et al., 2016; Lodder et al., 2017; Moeller & Seehuus, 2019). Experiencing shame behind this feeling of being isolated in the college experience can further amplify loneliness (Lim et al., 2016; Moeller & Seehuus, 2019)." (Wodika et al., 2024, p. 292)

As new and returning students head back to college and university campuses, it’s important they strive academically but it’s also important that students make efforts to connect socially to others—to make at least one friend. Graduate student Mikaela Dahlman and I recently wrote about loneliness in college students. Published in the Social and Emotional Learning Journal, we argued that college is a context rich with opportunities for students to hone their social and emotional competencies. Students whose social and emotional skills are well developed tend to fare better academically—researchers argue that students engage differently with course content (e.g., have the confidence to ask questions when stumped), interact cooperatively with fellow students, and build rapport with faculty (e.g., attend office hours, ask questions in class). One of the pillars of social and emotional learning (SEL) is social awareness that includes the ability to form and maintain friendships. In light of the high rates of loneliness, particularly in first-year students, the ability to make friends is especially important for thwarting compromised mental health on campus. Having at least one friend helps buffer well-being and mental health. I’d argue too that the college context provides ample opportunities for students to make friends, with many of these friendships carrying forward throughout adulthood.

A UBC therapy dog unites two students on campus
Source: Freya L. L. Green Photography; Used with permission

This fall, I’ll teach a class on social and emotional learning to 158 prospective teachers pursuing a Bachelor of Education at the University of British Columbia, Okanagan. As part of our class, I’ll ask students to “make a new friend”—to walk through the process of building rapport, perspective-taking to learn of another’s interests, and to discover common ground. This "befriending" intervention is a structured approach that typically connects someone who needs a friend with a supportive peer, with the goal that, over time and through a series of activities, a friendship emerges. Over the course of the semester, my students will both initiate and maintain a friendship. I want my students to participate in this activity so they are reminded of the clunky and often awkward steps involved in making a friend. Throughout the course, I’ll have my students reflect on this emerging friendship and the implications for their teaching. My hope is that these new teachers will have heightened awareness of the importance of fostering friendships in the students they’ll teach, have an understanding of the importance of friendship for mental well-being, and have a nuanced sense of the choreography of making a friend. In a future post, I'll report back on what my students said about our befriending activity and their thoughts on whether it informed (enriched?) their role as a teacher.

article continues after advertisement

Friendship is a much-discussed and researched topic, and readers curious to dive deeper into understanding friendship are directed to Psychology Today author Madora Kibbe, who recently wrote about “The importance of a few good friends" and a recent systematic review by Perzirkianidis and colleagues, which examined the link between friendship and well-being.

item.title: Why the Mind Needs an Afterlife
item.description:
Spirituality

Why the Mind Needs an Afterlife

The urge to believe in an afterlife is a defense against the fear of mortality.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • As humans, we understand our own mortality. The thought of permanent erasure leads to existential anxiety.
  • Faith in life after death provides a mental sanctuary, giving life meaning and direction.
  • Believing in an afterlife eases the fear of death with the promise that consciousness endures.

Our view of the afterlife demonstrates that the human urge to believe routinely beats the need for hard proof. That conviction is a double-edged sword: It provides vital comfort, but at a price. Uncritical belief can lead to denial and a false sense of security, prompting people to warp reality to protect their peace rather than face uncomfortable truths.

Still, faith provides vital survival benefits. It acts as a mental sanctuary, giving life meaning and direction. Essential to this comfort is belief in an afterlife and a notion of heaven—the idea that death isn't the absolute end, and consciousness isn't erased. This conviction serves several key purposes in our lives.

Assuaging the Dread of Nonexistence

Humans possess a unique level of self-awareness: We understand our own mortality. The thought of permanent erasure causes profound existential anxiety. Believing in a realm free from pain and suffering directly combats this fear, offering a promise of continuity rather than absolute annihilation.

Spanish philosopher Miguel de Unamuno wrote extensively about the "hunger for immortality." He argued that human reason tells us death is the end, but human passion and emotion desperately demand eternal life. For Unamuno, this conflict creates the core "tragic sense" of human existence, making the desire for an afterlife not a logical conclusion, but a vital emotional necessity to keep despair at bay.

Softening the Inevitability of Death

Although death remains an absolute biological certainty (at least for now), the sustained anticipation of mortality frequently manifests as a significant psychological burden in late life. Belief systems centered on an afterlife fulfill a protective, coping function by mitigating the acute anxiety associated with death. This concept aligns directly with the theories of cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker, who theorized that individuals formulate "immortality projects"—including spiritual frameworks, artistic legacies, and religious convictions—to grant their existence enduring significance and to mentally counter the prospect of total obliteration.

Making a Finite Existence Palatable

Without belief in an afterlife, human existence—emerging from nothing only to return to nothing—can feel bleak. Anticipating something beyond softens the harsh reality of our limited lifespan, reframing a brief life into part of an enduring journey.

Psychologist and philosopher William James highlighted the functional value of faith, arguing that believing in a higher order satisfies a core need for hope, safety, and meaning. For James, if believing in an afterlife helps someone process grief and find emotional stability in a harsh world, that belief holds genuine practical value and truth.

article continues after advertisement

Other benefits to seeking belief in an afterlife:

The Need to Preserve Loved Ones and Bonds: Grief and bereavement create a deep existential rupture. The belief in an afterlife reframes death not as an absolute, permanent termination of a relationship, but as a temporary interruption. This provides crucial psychological space to continue an emotional bond with the deceased, offering comfort during acute loss and maintaining a sense of ongoing connection.

Restoring Cosmic Justice and Fairness: The physical world is frequently indifferent and unequal—good deeds go unrewarded, suffering can feel arbitrary, and injustices often go unpunished in a person's lifetime. An afterlife satisfies a fundamental human desire for a moral universe. It creates a framework of ultimate accountability, where pain is transmuted into peace and ethical integrity carries lasting weight. “Cosmic justice” can give us comfort in the face of all the bad in the world.

Anchoring Identity, Agency, and Self-Worth: If human consciousness is completely extinguished at death, individual identity can feel fragile or impermanent. Believing in an afterlife reinforces a sense of personal agency and enduring self-worth, assuring the individual that their life's story is part of a permanent, meaningful trajectory rather than an accidental, temporary spark, in a sense, leaving a spiritual carbon footprint for posterity.

Social Cohesion and Shared Worldviews: On a cultural and community level, shared beliefs in an afterlife establish collective norms, moral structures, and shared rituals. This provides communities with a common language around dying, grieving, and memorializing, fostering social unity and mutual support when confronting life's finality. Misery doesn’t just love company; it needs company.

article continues after advertisement

Perspective at a Cosmic Scale: Ultimately, believing in an afterlife—or in a supreme creator—is less about objective divine truth and more about enduring our own existential dread. When confronted by a vast, indifferent universe in which our brief existence is a mere blip on the cosmic timeline, we naturally seek shelter in self-importance. We construct intricate afterlife narratives to reassure ourselves that we are not insignificant, that our suffering has purpose, and that consciousness will not simply be erased.

Yet herein lies the central paradox of the human condition: Even when confronted by the cold reality of science, mathematical improbability, and a universe governed solely by physical laws, our emotional compulsion to believe remains largely unshaken. Despite every piece of factual evidence pointing toward an impersonal cosmos, the human spirit continues to demand meaning, desperately clinging to hope.

item.title: Why Reasoning With an Upset Child Can Make Things Worse
item.description:
Anger

Why Reasoning With an Upset Child Can Make Things Worse

The more logical you are during a meltdown, the less your child may hear you.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • A highly upset child may temporarily be less able to hear you.
  • Repeating logical explanations can unintentionally fuel the emotional reactivity.
  • Parents can lower the temperature by saying less, not more.

Erin, a mom at her wits' end, looked at me pleadingly and said, "Dr. Jeff, what am I missing here? I was being completely reasonable with Paige" (names have been changed to protect privacy). Yes, Erin was being (as she saw it) reasonable as she replayed the recent chaotic episode featuring none other than twelve-year-old Paige.

By the way, the incident Erin was referring to was Paige's recent 12th birthday party. Oh, those wonderful memories that parents get to look back on. If you are wondering what the catalyst was that stoked Paige's ire, it was that her newly acquired birthday present, her new phone, came with some unexpected screen usage controls and time boundaries.

Why More Explanation Leads To Surges in Emotional Reactivity

In the above situation, Erin was shocked to see that her ordinary limit-setting had turned into a big-time blow-up with Paige. Erin learned an in-your-face, intense lesson: sometimes being super reasonable at the wrong time can make already upset children even more emotionally inflamed. That's because when children become intensely upset, their nervous systems go on a big-time emotional surge before the thinking part of their brains can catch up. I tell my clients that at this point, it is similar to trying to reason with an adult who is intoxicated.

What Not To Say

As I explain in my book, 24 Hours To A Less Reactive Child: The One-Day Reset to Reduce Conflict, Calm Big Emotions, and Reconnect, many caring parents start to talk more when their child is emotionally struggling. So if you picture doors slamming, refusing to speak, or totally shutting down, those aren't times to say certain things. Unless you want to pour kerosene on the reactivity fire, don't say things like: "We've already discussed this," "You know why I said no," or "Can you please just listen?"

Yes, I will admit these all sound like sensible sentences, but the big-time problem is you're appealing to your child's reactive brain at a time when it can't listen. In short, when your child is emotionally surging and you try to explain with logic, you add more pressure (because they can't truly process what you are saying), and they feel tons of pressure.

What To Do That Works Better

To help re-regulate your reactive child's emotions, first help them name them to tame them. For example, saying "You sound really upset right now" is something they can hear because it's true and it resonates. Next, think less is more: lower your volume, lower your intensity, and slow your speaking pace.

To help accomplish this, I encourage parents to imagine being suspended from the ceiling, looking down to see the whole interaction, rather than just hearing themselves speak. Last, hold your boundary without overexplaining it. For example, Erin realized that instead of simply saying "the phone stays downstairs tonight," she kept explaining and unwittingly fueling Paige's anger.

item.title: The 3 Causes of Human Suffering
item.description:
Spirituality

The 3 Causes of Human Suffering

How to break the cycle of not being present.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Suffering is a result of clinging, aversion, and ignorance.
  • Our unproductive habits keep us out of the present.
  • Letting go of our story is an important step toward a fulfilled life.

We admitted we were powerless over alcohol and our lives had become unmanageable. —The First Step, Alcoholics Anonymous

In late January, I sat for a 10-day silent meditation retreat in northern India. On the first day of the retreat, we were introduced to the three causes of suffering according to the Buddha. Two and a half thousand years ago, he said (and I am not quoting here; this is what I recall) that there are three causes of suffering:

  • Clinging
  • Aversion
  • Ignorance

Since that retreat, I have been deeply pondering this because it intersects with my work as a performance psychologist and with my personal history of addiction and recovery. What did Buddha mean by clinging, aversion, and ignorance?

Clinging

Clinging is simply what we're attached to: what we would like to happen, what we want things to be like. I want to be happy. I want to be rich. I want to be successful. But it can also be material things: I want that car. I want to live in that house. And it can be relationships. I want my children to be a certain way. I want my spouse to treat me better. I want my boss to be nicer.

Aversion

Aversion is the opposite. It's when we don't want something. I don't like that it's cold outside. I don't like the way my co-worker speaks to me. I don't like that I have limited funds. I don't like this. I don't like that. It's anything we wish were different because we're not happy, satisfied, or fulfilled with what is.

Ignorance

Ignorance, the third cause of human suffering, is a bit more opaque. At least it was to me at first. However, as I contemplated it more, I came to understand, in my own way, what Buddha meant. Ignorance—and again, this is my own interpretation—is the failure to recognize that everything is in a constant state of flux and change, which means that every moment is a new moment. Every breath is a new breath.

Think about a movie (if you still go to the movies). What you're watching on the screen looks like a continuous story, but really it's one frame after another, after another, after another, going on for an hour and a half, two hours, or more. Each frame is a moment. Stringing them together creates the story.

In fact, during the first 10 minutes of the retreat, I had a realization: There's the moment, and then there's the story about the moment.

This reminded me of a Laurie Anderson lyric: This is the time. And this is the record of the time. Each moment is singular; linking them together is the record.

What this means is that we create a story and then we get attached to it. We like it—clinging. We don't like it—aversion. Our lives become a story we tell ourselves, really just a stringing together of individual moments over a long period of time.

article continues after advertisement

Performance and the Present Moment

How does this relate to my work as a performance psychologist?

For the past 40 years, I have focused on what people need to do to perform at their best. I work with elite athletes, surgeons, first responders, and others who must perform at their peak under intense pressure.

The central core of my work is presence: being in the present.

On a certain level, it doesn't matter how the Olympic swimmer did in her last meet or how she's going to perform tomorrow. What matters is right now, this moment, and pouring all of her skill, talent, and drive into it. Shaquille O’Neal could make free throws in practice, but under the pressure of the present moment, he struggled to do what he already knew how to do, shooting just 52.7 percent from the free-throw line over his career. Clinging to what happened before, avoiding what is happening now, and forgetting that every moment is a new moment—all of these take us out of the present.

Lately, I have been focusing my work as a performance psychologist on visionary founders, people who have a genuine vision for a product or service that could genuinely help humanity, particularly those who could not otherwise afford the goods or services that privileged people can. But founders are under enormous pressure and may revert to addictive habits of alcohol, drugs, pornography, gambling, or some other behavior to get away from what they are feeling. Instead of facing what is happening right now, they escape it. We work to break through unproductive habits that have developed through clinging, aversion, and ignorance so they can be fully present to deal with each challenge as it arises, no matter how big or small, no matter if it's wanted or unwanted.

Addiction and Recovery

I have learned this through my own story as well: overcoming two addictions and being in recovery for 37 years, regularly attending 12-step meetings.

The wisdom in "one day at a time" reflects what Buddha was talking about. Each day is new. Every day affords possibility.

Certainly, clinging and aversion run very deep in any addictive process. Speaking personally, after hearing the stories of countless people over the years, one deep root of addiction is that we're unhappy with our circumstances and our lives, and we seek quick relief through alcohol, drugs, pornography, gambling, shopping, however we can get a “hit.”

article continues after advertisement

So we have this toxic cycle: aversion ("I can't stand my life, I don't like myself"), clinging ("This is what I need to make me feel better"), and ignorance (“I’ll never get out of this”).

The only way to break out of the cycle is one day at a time, one action at a time, moment by moment: not to have the drink, not to log on to the pornography website, not to place another bet.

Now. Right now. In the present. Bring the cause of suffering—ignorance—out of the shadows and into the light: What is the story I keep telling myself? How do I rerun that story over and over again?

The Freedom of This Moment

To keep ourselves from sinking in the quicksand of our stories (“I always want to be this happy” [clinging]; “My life’s a mess, I can’t stand it anymore” [aversion]), we need to break through our ignorance about how life works. It’s one fresh moment after another. It is the inhale and then the exhale. The blink of an eye. The touch of the breeze upon our face.

We can break through the chains of our controlling story-driven self. We can live the life we were created to have.

Right now.
